extractor.note: Extraction focused on core doctrine and application of intentionality across the commentary. Chapter Two introduces intentionality as the first structural feature of transcendental consciousness; Chapter Three applies intentional analysis to perception and flesh; Chapter Four examines constitution through intentional life. Partial coverage of remaining chapters (Five-Twelve) for thematic richness and development.

coverage_note: Covers the introduction and core doctrine of intentionality across Chapters One-Four with emphasis on: Ch. Two §§123-125 (intentionality as first structure), Ch. Three §§139-163 (intentional analysis, noematic correlation, horizon-structure), Ch. Four §169 (constitution through intentional life). Also covers selected passages from Chapters Five-Seven establishing intentionality in relation to eidetic analysis, idealism, and solipsism. Not fully covered: later applications in Chapters Eight-Twelve, the full development of intentionality through alterity and pairing.

units.claim: Intentionality is the first fundamental structure of the transcendental field, brought out by shifting focus from singular ego-positing to the multiple acts of consciousness.
units.quote: By shifting the center of gravity of transcendental evidence from the *ego cogito* (the singular act of self-positing) to the multiple *cogitationes* (the multiple acts of consciousness), the phenomenologist brings out the first of these structures: intentionality.

units.claim: Intentionality is defined as the universal fundamental property of consciousness: to be consciousness of something, bearing its cogitatum within itself.
units.quote: Franck cites Husserl: the word intentionality means nothing other than this universal fundamental property of consciousness — to be consciousness of something, as a cogito to bear within itself its cogitatum.

units.claim: The intentional correlate (noema) is the object-as-perceived held within the cogitatio in an irreal sense, distinct from the real object.
units.quote: Each lived experience of consciousness is a consciousness of …, regardless of whether its object actually exists. The relation to the perceived, for example, is essential to perception itself; it contains the *cogitatum* (the perceived as perceived) in an irreal sense within the *cogitatio*.

units.claim: Reflection is itself an intentional process that relates back to the original lived experience, making the original available as the correlate of reflective consciousness.
units.quote: The reflective attitude yields a new intentional process, one with the peculiarity of "relating back to the earlier process" (*Rückbeziehung auf das frühere Erlebnis*), and this new process is awareness — even, possibly, evidential awareness — of just that earlier process itself, and not of any other.

units.claim: Consciousness is intentionally correlative with its objects, establishing a dual-oriented analysis examining both the noema and the noeses.
units.quote: The demonstration that consciousness is intentionally correlative with its objects forces a dual orientation onto the analysis of consciousness — a correlative structure.

units.claim: Intentional analysis is the analysis of transcendental subjectivity insofar as it constitutes all possible objectivity through noetic-noematic correlation.
units.quote: Intentional analysis is thus the analysis of the transcendental ego insofar as the ego includes and constitutes all possible objectivity.

units.claim: Phenomenology necessarily begins with intentional analysis of perception as its exemplary case, responding to the deep necessity of overcoming transcendental psychologism.
units.quote: If phenomenology is always a phenomenology of perception, this is for essential and profoundly historical reasons. Franck cites Husserl: involuntarily, he says, we began with the intentional analysis of perception — and indeed gave privileged status to intuitively given physical bodies (*Körper*).

units.claim: The intentional object is the identical unity of various modes of noetic-noematic consciousness, unified through synthetic relations.
units.quote: What was just found — in the exemplary analysis of perception, which holds *mutatis mutandis* for all conscious life — can be condensed thus: the intentional object as such is conscious as the identical unity of various modes of noetic-noematic consciousness; conscious life is essentially synthetic.

units.claim: Internal time-consciousness is the fundamental form of synthesis underlying intentional relations, joining lived experiences into a continuous flow.
units.quote: And in the final analysis, internal time-consciousness is the fundamental form of this synthesis. The phenomenology of perception implies a phenomenology of temporality that joins lived experiences together into a single, unique flow.

units.claim: Conscious life exhibits a reflexive intentional relatedness to itself, demonstrating intentionality as the being-for-itself characteristic of consciousness.
units.quote: The fact is evident — even apodictically evident — and indicates one aspect of the ego's marvellous being-for-himself: above all the being of his conscious life in the form of reflexive intentional relatedness to himself.

units.claim: The horizon-structure is an essential feature of intentionality insofar as intentionality is the positing of objects; every object is given within horizons that generate further horizons.
units.quote: The horizon-structure remains an essential feature of intentionality insofar as intentionality is positing of objects. Every cogitatum is given within a horizon that in turn gives rise to new horizons; therefore the sense of the object — the noema — can never be given as something complete.

units.claim: Intentional analysis unfolds the constitutive syntheses underlying each actuality, inquiring back to the multiplicities of noetic syntheses that continually constitute objects.
units.quote: It is not a real (psychological) analysis — there is no empiricist sensualism of intentionality; rather, it unfolds, distinguishes, and clarifies the richness of horizons and infinite potentialities harboured and concealed in each actuality.

units.claim: The intentional object serves as a transcendental clue for displaying constitutive noetic structures, grounding the method of intentional analysis itself.
units.quote: First, the intentional object must serve as a *transcendental clue* for displaying the constitutive noetic structures. This affirms a relative and methodological privilege of the constituted (in phenomenology, the question of method is sovereign).

units.claim: Being and non-being, reality and irreality, are constituted in and through intentional life; the reduction reveals being as wholly reducible to intentional sense.
units.quote: It is therefore necessary to show that being and non-being, reality and irreality, are constituted in and through intentional life — such that, as Husserl says, the idea of investigating anything outside the parentheses placed by the reduction "cannot occur to us within the sphere of phenomenological reduction."

units.claim: The fifth Meditation poses the question of the being of intentionality in relation to the constitution of objectivity and intersubjectivity.
units.quote: In short, the fifth Meditation treats the *objectivity of the object*, thereby posing the question of *the being of intentionality*.

units.claim: Each cogito intends more than what is actually given (the Mehrmeinung); this supplementary intentional aim is essential to intentional analysis itself.
units.quote: This means that each cogito intends *more* than what is actually there (the *Mehrmeinung*, the "meaning-more"), and without this supplementary aim intentional analysis could not even take place — could not inquire back to the multiplicities of noetic syntheses that continually give the object as the same.

units.claim: The object is a pole of identity constituted by multiple intentional syntheses; it serves as the organizing center for the correlative system of consciousness.
units.quote: The object is a pole of identity, an index of noetic constitutive intentionalities. At the same time, intentional analysis acquires a distinctive structure.
